subject: system-design
title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal
summary: The two fundamental ways to add capacity to a system, and the tradeoffs that push most real systems toward scaling out.

blocks.text: When a system can no longer keep up with its load, you have two fundamental moves: make one machine bigger, or add more machines. Almost every scaling decision is a variation on this choice.
Vertical scaling means giving a single machine more resources — more CPU, more RAM, faster disks. The application doesn't change; it simply runs on a beefier box.

items: Simplest path: no code changes, no distributed-systems problems.
One machine means one source of truth — no coordination overhead.
Great early on, when a bigger instance is one config change away.

blocks.title: The ceiling
blocks.text: There is a largest machine money can buy, and cost climbs faster than capacity near the top. A single box is also a single point of failure.
Horizontal scaling means adding more machines and spreading the load across them, usually behind a load balancer. Capacity grows by adding commodity nodes rather than buying a bigger one.

items: No hard ceiling: keep adding nodes as traffic grows.
Redundancy is built in — one node failing doesn't take the system down.
But now state must be shared or partitioned, which is the hard part.

blocks.text: Stateless services scale out almost for free. The difficulty is always the stateful layer — the database and the cache.

Scale up first: it buys time cheaply and keeps the design simple. Plan to scale out before the ceiling forces your hand — design services to be stateless early, so adding nodes later is a deployment change, not a rewrite.
